title: The ZigZag
summary: Avoid the rook’s skewers, walk behind the opposing king, and defend against mate after promotion.

nodes.question: How can two separated pawns defeat a rook?
nodes.explanation: Immediate f8=Q permits a skewer. Advancing a6 first creates two promotion threats, but White still needs a careful king route.

nodes.question: What must the new queen defend?
nodes.explanation: The rook has captured f7 and threatens ...Rf8 mate. White must keep both its king and queen safe instead of assuming that promotion finishes the game.

branches.title: Zigzag into shelter, then prevent mate
commentary: Begin from the complete five-piece source board. The encoded checking route follows the saved diagrams.
a7 creates a second immediate promotion threat, so the rook cannot simply focus on the f-pawn.
Kb6 approaches a7 and keeps contact with the queenside passer.
Ke5 moves away from f7 to deny Black the shoulder-and-skewer idea. If the king goes to c5 now, f8=Q comes with check.
Re1+ starts the illustrated checking defense along the e-file.
Kd6 steps diagonally toward the queenside shelter while leaving both pawns on the seventh rank.
Rd1+ shifts the checking file to follow the white king.
Ke7 zigzags back toward the eighth rank, avoiding being driven directly in front of a new queen.
Re1+ renews the file check in the source’s selected sequence.
Kd8 crosses onto the eighth rank. The rook must change files to keep checking.
Rd1+ follows the king once more.
Kc8 continues across the eighth rank toward the shelter created by Kb6.
Rc1+ is the last illustrated file check before White reaches b8.
Kb8 shelters on the b-file: Black’s king on b6 blocks a rook check from below.
Rf1 turns to the f-pawn and sets up one last tactical trap after the other pawn promotes.
a8=Q promotes the queenside pawn. White has achieved a queen, but its king remains boxed near the corner.
Rxf7 captures the remaining pawn and threatens ...Rf8 mate, using Kb6 to cover a7, b7 and c7.
Qa3 guards f8 along the a3–f8 diagonal, meeting ...Rf8+ with Qxf8. The exact queen-versus-rook ending is winning for White; further conversion is outside this selected line.

branches.title: Promote before creating the second threat
commentary: Compare the source’s immediate f-pawn promotion.
f8=Q gives up White’s forced win by allowing the rook to check along the f-file.
Rf1+ skewers the king and new queen, forcing the king off that file.
Ke7 is the illustrated retreat; the queen is left on f8.
Rxf8 captures the queen, reducing White’s attack to the distant a-pawn.
Kxf8 takes the rook, reaching a king-and-pawn ending.
Kb6 approaches the a6 pawn. The tablebase confirms a draw with correct play; White cannot force that remaining pawn through.

branches.title: Ignore the rook’s mating threat
commentary: Compare the illustrated queen centralization instead of defending f8.
Qd5 abandons the necessary defense against the back-rank attack. The exact outcome reverses to a Black win.
Rf8+ checks along the eighth rank. Black retains a checked forced win; this branch stops here rather than inventing an unillustrated mating sequence.

exercises.prompt: Why is a new queen not enough?
exercises.answer: The king on b8 has no useful flight against ...Rf8: Kb6 controls the seventh-rank escapes and Qa8 occupies the corner. Qa3 must defend the checking square.

exercises.prompt: What does Ke5 gain by abandoning f7?
exercises.answer: It avoids the opposing king’s shoulder tactic and puts Kc5 in line with f8=Q+, giving White time to promote with check.
